newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav firms' insolvency on the rise - experts.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav firms' insolvency on the rise - experts.

text.p: Insolvency among Yugoslav firms is growing and unless concrete steps are taken soon the economy will be struggling for bare survival, the Yugoslav Chamber of Commerce has warned.

"Unless adequate economic measures are taken within the next few months, the economy could virtually find itself under a complete blockade," Dimitrije Tucovic sugar refinery director Milorad Bojkovic told this year's first meeting of the Chamber's Economy Committee on Wednesday.
According to the National Bank of Yugoslavia's data, a total of 21,927 firms were insolvent on January 31, 1997.

Although the firms represent a small percentage of the total number, they employ some 522,000 people, or a fifth of the total number of employed registered by official statistics. Statistics do not cover the private sector.
Outstanding liabilites of the firms stood at around 6.513 billion dinars ($1.18 billion), up 129 percent compared to December 31, 1996, the central bank report said.
Receivership proceedings have been instituted for 1,076 firms employing 11,561 people, and proposed for another 16,000.
"Clearly there has been no improvement in liquidity compared to the end of last year. In fact it has deteriorated," Chamber official Milija Milojevic said.
Only a third of the workforce is actually working while the rest are waiting to receive their guaranteed minimum wages, Bojkovic said.
Firms have to pay one dinar in taxes for every dinar of wages for all employees, including those who are on "compulsory leave" since most industry is operating at half capacity.
Instead of the promised unburdening, the tax burden on firms has actually increased, because they are paying taxes on non-productive workers as well, Bojkovic said.
Financial police have become more rigorous in freezing the accounts of insolvent firms, so the bulk of the economy could find itself totally blocked soon, he said.

"It is the last moment for the authors of economic policy to face this reality. We cannot act like ostriches and stick our heads in the sand," Bojkovic said. -- Amra Kevic, Belgrade newsroom +381 11 222 4305
